title: Luria–Delbrück Experiment
description: Testing random versus adaptive mutation with fluctuation analysis, colony counts, and sequence comparisons

blocks.text:
Write a summary of this experiment, its objectives, and conclusions between one paragraph and one page in length.

The goal of this experiment is to find out whether mutations occur randomly (random mutation hypothesis) or when exposed to environmental stress (adaptive immunity hypothesis). We used S.cerevisiae yeast to test how it acquires antifungal resistance to Canavanine. The theory is that if the adaptive immunity hypothesis is correct, mutations occur only after the yeast comes in contact with canavanine, which we would expect a low variance in the number of resistant colonies that appear on each plate. However, if the random mutation hypothesis is correct, and the mutations develop prior to canavanine exposure, the number of mutations on each plate would vary wildly. 

We first count the number of yeast cells using a hemocytometer and brightfield microscope, which helps us calculate the density/concentration of yeast cells. Then we plate 27 cultures of these cells (100µL) onto dry agar plates that contain canavanine. The plates are incubated at 30c for 2 days, which then colonies are counted. PCR is then performed on mutated yeast colonies that developed canavanine resistance. The CAN1 gene produces a protein that carries canavanine across the cell barrier, and mutations on this gene are what allows yeast to survive on the selective media. Therefore we will focus on the CAN1 region of the genome.

Our experiment aligns with the random mutation hypothesis. The large fano factor calculated suggests that mutations occurred randomly and not due to exposure to canavanine. The sequencing of the genome also shows us the genetic changes (multiple different types) that allows for S.cerevisiae to be resistant to canavanine.

In this problem, we will simulate mutations among populations of cells for the adaptive immunity hypothesis and for the random mutation hypothesis.

a)Starting with 1000 non-mutated cells and a mutation rate of 10^-5 mutations
per cell division, run a computer simulation of mutations over the course of
several generations. Do this at least 100 times each for both the adaptive immunity hypothesis and for the random mutation hypothesis.

b)Plot the probability distributions (P(n; N) vs. n) for each hypothesis, where n
is the number of mutant cells present at the end of the simulation and N is the
total number of cells.

c)Calculate the mean, variance, and Fano factors for each hypothesis.

d)For which hypothesis is the distribution binomial? Does this jibe with the discussion in the Background section?
